questions.problem: Find the integral of $\frac{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}{\sqrt{{x}^{5}}}-5{x}^{-1}$ with respect to $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
Simplifying the exponents and applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}{\sqrt{{x}^{5}}}-5{x}^{-1})\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{5/2-3/2}}\,\text{d}x-5\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x-5\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the integral of ${(2-\frac{1}{x})}^{2}$ with respect to $x.$

Expanding the binomial and applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(2-\frac{1}{x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =\int (4-\frac{4}{x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & =\int 4\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{4}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\int \text{d}x-4\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4x-4ln⁡|x|+\frac{{x}^{-2+1}}{-2+1}+C \\  & =4x-4ln⁡|x|-\frac{1}{x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Expanding the binomial and applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1+\frac{1}{x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =\int (1+\frac{2}{x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x+2\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x+2ln⁡|x|+\frac{{x}^{-2+1}}{-2+1}+C \\  & =x+2ln⁡|x|-\frac{1}{x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=2ln⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $2ln⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1+\frac{1}{x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =x-\frac{1}{x}+2ln⁡|x|+2ln⁡K \\  & =x-\frac{1}{x}+2(ln⁡|x|+ln⁡K) \\  & =x-\frac{1}{x}+2ln⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the integral of $\dfrac 1 {2x} + 3x$ with respect to $x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{1}{2x}+3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2x}\,\text{d}x+\int 3x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+3\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}ln⁡|x|+3\cdot \frac{{x}^{1+1}}{1+1}+C \\  & =\frac{ln⁡|x|}{2}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We separate the integrand into the sum of two fractions so that we can simplify each term. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3+2x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{3}{x}+\frac{2x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{3}{x}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+2\int \,\text{d}x \\  & =3ln⁡|x|+2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C =3 \ln K$ where $K$ is some other constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $3\ln|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3+2x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =3ln⁡|x|+2x+C \\  & =3ln⁡|x|+2x+3ln⁡K \\  & =3ln⁡(K|x|)+2x.\end{aligned}
$$
